Dead-registration snippet: matching on raw HTTP 404 is risky; prefer details[].errorCode === 'UNREGISTERED' (FcmError). The regex on the 400 message can match BadRequest field violations such as "Invalid value at 'message.token'", so only treat a 400 as dead when details holds an FcmError and no google.rpc.BadRequest.

Two different HTTP 401s must be told apart. An invalid or expired OAuth token gives 401 with status UNAUTHENTICATED and no details (probed live); the fix is to clear the cached token and retry once, which the snippet does not do. THIRD_PARTY_AUTH_ERROR is also HTTP 401 and is identified by details[].errorCode.
THIRD_PARTY_PERMISSION_DENIED (HTTP 403, web push) exists. FCM considers a registration stale after one month without connecting and recommends pruning stored FIDs by their last-upload timestamp.

android_v2 (AndroidConfigV2) is a pre-GA preview that needs an EAP Android SDK (firebase-messaging 26.1.0-eap01 from a local Maven repo). It cannot be combined with `android` in the same request, so do not use it in this project.

Google's service-account doc has an addendum: APIs whose service definition is published in googleapis accept a self-signed JWT (aud=https://SERVICE.googleapis.com/) directly as the bearer, skipping the token exchange. Whether FCM accepts this was not verified.

Flutter snippet bugs: the getAPNSToken()==null branch does not return, so register() still runs before the APNs token exists. Each enablePush() call adds another onRegistered/onUnregistered listener (duplicate uploads) unless the subscriptions are kept and cancelled. register() itself prompts for permission.

The WebCrypto and jose paths were tested only on the Deno 2.9.6 CLI, not on the Supabase Edge Runtime. The official Supabase guide imports a bundled ../service-account.json; keeping the key in a Supabase secret (as the report does) avoids committing it. The guide triggers the function from a database webhook and deploys it with --no-verify-jwt.
HTTP v1 sends one message per request (no multicast in the REST API). The project quota is 600K quota tokens per minute; QUOTA_EXCEEDED needs backoff starting at 1 minute or more.

The FCM `data` map rejects non-string values with 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT/BadRequest (official example: "Invalid value at 'message.data[0].value' (TYPE_STRING), 12"), so the Edge Function must stringify order IDs and similar values.

@supabase/server rejects legacy anon/service_role keys and legacy HS256 user JWTs. auth:'user' requires a 'kid' in the token header, i.e. asymmetric JWT signing keys. If the project still signs user tokens with the legacy JWT secret, auth:'user' fails with INVALID_JWT, so check or migrate the project's JWT signing keys first (package docs/auth-modes.md).

@supabase/server pitfalls. A malformed SUPABASE_SECRET_KEYS silently resolves to {}. Bare auth:'secret' matches only the key named 'default' and never falls back to named keys. The secret_key stored in Vault for pg_cron must therefore be the 'default' secret key, or the function must use 'secret:<name>' / 'secret:*'. Rotating or renaming the default key breaks cron calls until Vault is updated.

Security caveat on the official cron pattern: pg_net writes the decrypted secret key into net.http_request_queue until the request is sent, and any role that can log in to the database can read it (schedule-functions.md caution). Also, anyone who can select from vault.decrypted_secrets sees plaintext.

pg_net's default 2000 ms timeout may be shorter than an Edge Function cold start plus run time; the cron quickstart example uses timeout_milliseconds:=5000. pg_net does not retry failed requests. Failures are visible only in net._http_response for 6 h, so dispatch logic should be idempotent and re-pick pending work on the next tick.

cron.job_run_details is never cleaned automatically, even after unschedule, so add a cleanup job. Supabase recommends at most 8 concurrent jobs, each under 10 minutes. Job names are case sensitive and can't be renamed.

Flutter uploadBinary/upload return the API 'Key', which includes the bucket id (e.g. 'price-lists/<wid>/<uuid>.pdf'). Store the bucket-relative path you passed in, not the return value, when later calling createSignedUrl/download, or the bucket name ends up doubled.

Price lists or other private documents should use public=false and serve files through createSignedUrl (SELECT policy needed). Optionally set file_size_limit/allowed_mime_types on the bucket.
Deleting rows from storage.objects with SQL does not delete the underlying file, which stays billed. Deletes must go through the Storage API (schema/design.md).

missing: Timeouts vs Supabase limits: Opus 5.5 at medium effort, emitting thinking plus about 100-150 JSON rows, can easily run past 150 s. The function must start returning a response, or hand the work to EdgeRuntime.waitUntil with a DB status row or Realtime update, before the 150 s request idle timeout. Total work is still capped at 150 s wall clock on Free and 400 s on paid. The snippet's client (timeout 300_000 ms, maxRetries 2) can wait up to about 15 min, far beyond either cap. Size the timeout, the retries and the chunk size to the plan's wall clock.

Server-side fallback changes the response shape. content starts with a {type:'fallback'} block. After a mid-stream decline, the fallback model continues from the partial text, so the JSON can be split across text blocks on either side of the fallback block. Code must join the text blocks, not read 'the' text block. SDK parse() would throw here because it parses each text block separately. The docs do not say whether the default fallback model keeps the json_schema grammar when it resumes mid-JSON; test this or treat it as a validation failure and retry.

Detecting which model served: read response.model and usage.iterations (a fallback_message entry). Sticky routing can send later requests straight to the fallback model for about 1 h. The docs recommend logging refusals and fallback-served responses as their own metrics, because both are HTTP 200.

Image resolution and cost: Opus 5.5 (Claude 4.7+) uses the high-resolution tier, max 2,576 px long edge and up to 4,784 visual tokens per image, and downscales anything larger. Resizing client-side to 2,576 px or less cuts upload size and function memory with no quality loss.

PDF pages are always fitted to the Standard tier (at most 1,568 visual tokens per page), even on Opus 5.5. A dense, small-font scanned price list may read better if each page is rendered and sent as an image at up to 2,576 px.
HEIC is not accepted. iPhone camera photos default to HEIC, so the mobile app should convert to JPEG before upload; rejecting on the server alone gives poor UX.

Memory budget: a 256 MB function holding the raw upload, its base64 copy (+33%), the JSON request body and the SDK buffers can run out on large PDFs. Consider uploading to Supabase Storage and streaming the file, or the Anthropic Files API (GA, no beta header) with a file_id reference.

The 2 s CPU-per-worker limit also covers SheetJS parsing, base64 encoding and zod validation. Large workbooks (tens of thousands of rows, many sheets) may exceed it. The report's 200 ms per 5,000 rows was measured on a dev machine, not on the edge runtime.
